title: Lighthouse or Landgrab? How to Pick Your AI Sales Strategy | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z argues enterprise AI startups face a binary go-to-market choice: a Lighthouse motion (win a few marquee logos to manufacture social proof) or a Landgrab motion (win on ROI math and maximum coverage), and that the choice is determined by two variables only — how much personal career exposure the signing buyer carries, and whether social proof travels in that market. The authors claim the more common error right now is defaulting to Lighthouse simply because AI feels new, burning months and cash chasing Fortune 100 logos while competitors take the fragmented mid-market.

themes.theme: The two-playbook framework for enterprise AI GTM

insights.claim: There are exactly two viable enterprise GTM playbooks for AI companies — Lighthouse (win marquee customers for social proof) and Landgrab (win on ROI math and sign the most customers possible) — and the correct choice is determined by what you sell and who you sell to, not by product quality or team strength.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: A diligence lens for AI startup investing: a mismatch between market type and sales motion is a leading indicator of stalled ARR regardless of product quality.
insights.quote: There are two GTM playbooks for AI companies selling into the enterprise: the Lighthouse and the Landgrab. The difference between them isn’t about product quality or team strength. It’s about what you’re selling and who you’re selling to.
insights.locator: There are two GTM playbooks for AI companies

insights.claim: The most common current mistake among AI founders is assuming buyers need social proof merely because the technology is AI and therefore feels new, when many buyers already understand the problem and only need the economics to work.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Watch for AI startups burning rounds on logo-chasing; the ones selling on demonstrable ROI into fragmented markets should compound revenue faster.
insights.quote: The more common mistake right now is the opposite: assuming buyers need proof just because the technology is AI and therefore feels new.
insights.locator: Sales cycles can provide another gut check

insights.claim: Chasing marquee logos actively destroys market position because founders offer steep discounts or even pay customers to adopt, generating revenue that barely registers while the buyers who would pay full price never hear of the company.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Discount-heavy marquee deals inflate logo slides but understate true ACV; scrutinize revenue quality and net pricing in AI startup metrics.
insights.quote: They just need the math to work, and every week spent chasing prestigious logos is a week a competitor spends selling in Ohio.
insights.locator: It’s not that there’s no logic to this

themes.theme: Buyer exposure as the dominant variable

insights.claim: Buyer exposure rises with three specific factors — whether the industry is regulated enough that a vendor mistake becomes the buyer's compliance problem, whether the product replaces a system of record versus sitting alongside one, and whether the output faces the outside world rather than an internal reviewer.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Score any enterprise AI target on these three axes to predict sales cycle length and CAC before looking at the pipeline.
insights.locator: How exposed is the buyer who signs?

insights.claim: In law and financial services all three exposure factors run hot, so ROI math is irrelevant to the buyer — they are managing personal career downside that no discount can offset.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Price cuts are wasted spend in high-exposure verticals; reference customers are the only unlock, so watch logo cadence not discounting.
insights.quote: For those buyers, the ROI math is beside the point. They’re managing personal downside no discount can offset.
insights.locator: In law and financial services all three run hot

insights.claim: When budget availability and napkin ROI point toward landgrab but buyer exposure points toward lighthouse, exposure wins every time — a buyer can have the budget, see the math, and still refuse to move until someone credible goes first.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Funded budget lines are not a sufficient signal of near-term conversion in high-exposure verticals; discount pipeline coverage accordingly.
insights.quote: When the two point in opposite directions, exposure wins every time.
insights.locator: Markets don’t always fall cleanly into one bucket

insights.claim: Sales cycles longer than 60 days, custom work to prove the concept, and buyers asking 'is this safe?' before 'what does it cost?' are diagnostic signals that a company is in lighthouse territory whether or not it planned to be.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: A concrete, checkable diagnostic to apply to any AI startup's actual sales data during diligence.
insights.quote: If they run longer than 60 days, if you’re doing custom work to prove the concept, if the buyer asks “is this safe?” before “what does it cost?”, your buyers need proof, and you need to run the lighthouse.
insights.locator: Sales cycles can provide another gut check

insights.claim: Common heuristics like 'SMB skews landgrab' or 'risk-averse industries skew lighthouse' are downstream artifacts — traced back far enough, every one of them reduces to exposure or proof, and the industry code on the account is irrelevant.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Segment AI GTM by exposure and proof-transfer rather than by company size or SIC code, which mis-sorts edge cases.
insights.quote: The controller at a 200-person distributor is a landgrab buyer because her market is fragmented and her deal is small. The industry code on the account never entered into it.
insights.locator: You’ll notice other patterns that seem to predict the motion

themes.theme: Whether social proof travels between buyers

insights.claim: In financial services and law, firms watch each other obsessively and status is legible, so landing two marquee firms moves the whole market because whoever went first has effectively performed the risk assessment for everyone behind them.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: In concentrated status-driven verticals, the second and third marquee logo are the real inflection point for revenue acceleration — a timing signal for entry.
insights.locator: Does social proof travel?

insights.claim: In fragmented mid-market segments like accounts receivable, a marquee logo buys almost nothing because buyers do not watch each other and each sale starts from zero on the math.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: For fragmented markets, sales headcount and coverage economics, not brand-name references, are the metric that predicts growth.
insights.quote: In AR at mid-market firms, the controller in Des Moines does not care that a household-name brand uses your product and is never going to hear about it anyway.
insights.locator: Does social proof travel?

insights.claim: A four-quadrant map falls out of exposure and proof-transfer: where proof travels but is not required, the product spreads itself engineer-to-engineer with a small sales team and category creation happens bottom-up, as with dev tools; where proof is required but logos never reach the buyer, the market is effectively unwinnable and the companies stuck there stay unknown.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Identifies a structurally dead quadrant — high-proof-required plus non-traveling proof — worth screening out of AI investments entirely.
insights.quote: Finally, when the buyer needs proof but the logos never reach them, you’re in a hard market and you likely haven’t heard of the companies stuck there.
insights.locator: Put these two questions together and you have the map

themes.theme: Lighthouse proof points: Harvey and Hebbia

insights.claim: Harvey created the AI-for-legal category from zero customers by landing Allen & Overy in late 2022 and Paul Weiss in early 2023, and now has hundreds of millions in ARR at an $11 billion valuation.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Concrete benchmark for how fast a lighthouse motion can compound in a status-driven vertical; also flags displacement risk for Thomson Reuters and LexisNexis research franchises.
insights.quote: Today Harvey has hundreds of millions in ARR and an $11 billion valuation, but it first needed A&O and Paul Weiss to tell the legal industry AI-powered legal work was real.
insights.locator: Harvey built AI for legal professionals

insights.claim: Hebbia broke into financial services via the world's largest private equity firms, hedge funds and consultancies, and has since expanded to more than 40% of the largest asset managers by AUM including KKR and BlackRock.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Demonstrates AI penetration depth already achieved inside buy-side workflows — a read-through on headcount and margin structure at large asset managers.
insights.locator: Hebbia ran the same playbook in financial services

insights.claim: Lighthouse selling is structurally expensive and unscalable by design: small-team, founder-led and high-touch, with six- to seven-figure ACVs, three-to-six-month or longer sales cycles, and the same team closing the deal and delivering the product.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Expect poor early sales efficiency ratios in genuine lighthouse companies; judge them on ACV and logo quality rather than magic number.
insights.quote: The team that closes the deal is often the same team that delivers the product, which is expensive and unscalable by design.
insights.locator: Capturing lighthouses is a small-team, founder-led

themes.theme: Landgrab proof points: Stuut, Decagon, and speed versus incumbents

insights.claim: In markets where the buyer already knows the problem, AI startups compete not only with other startups but with incumbents adding AI each quarter, so distribution must be won before the incumbent achieves innovation.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: The window for AI-native challengers in known-problem categories is closing quarter by quarter as incumbents ship AI; time-to-coverage is the key variable to track.
insights.quote: In the words of our colleague Alex Rampell: you need to get distribution before the incumbent gets innovation.
insights.locator: In these markets, sacrificing speed is deadly

insights.claim: Stuut deliberately targeted the lower middle market over Fortune 100 logos in accounts receivable, delivering 40% higher cash flow, 70% fewer manual tasks and a 37% shorter collection period while deploying in under a week versus the 6 to 18 months of a traditional rollout.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Deployment time compression from months to days is the wedge against SAP, Oracle and HighRadius AR modules — a direct threat to legacy ERP add-on revenue.
insights.quote: customers increase cash flow by 40%, cut manual tasks by 70%, and lower their collection period by 37%
insights.locator: Take Stuut, which automates accounts receivable

insights.claim: Decagon ran roughly a hundred customer conversations in a month before building its product, then scaled from zero to eight figures of ARR in 18 months and signed more than 100 new enterprise customers in 2025 alone, tripling its valuation to $4.5 billion in under six months.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: A benchmark growth curve for AI agents replacing whole functions rather than augmenting them; also a marker of how fast private AI valuations are re-rating.
insights.quote: In 2025 alone, the company signed more than 100 new enterprise customers across travel, finance, health, and retail, tripling its valuation to $4.5 billion in under six months.
insights.locator: Decagon used a similar motion to win in customer support

insights.claim: Landgrab selling requires a standardized product, a larger demo-driven sales team, and forward-deployed implementation teams specialized in delivery rather than discovery, with unit economics that must work at volume.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Product standardization and gross margin at volume are the make-or-break metrics for landgrab AI companies, not deal size.
insights.quote: The unit economics have to work at volume because volume is the whole strategy.
insights.locator: Landgrab selling is demo-driven

themes.theme: Failure modes specific to each motion

insights.claim: Lighthouse companies risk becoming hostage to the logo, fighting over the same roughly 500 accounts every other AI startup is pitching while those accounts extract concessions knowing the seller is desperate — when the vast majority of revenue sits in companies no one has heard of.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Crowding into the same ~500 enterprise accounts compresses AI startup pricing power; the unbranded long tail is the underpriced opportunity.
insights.quote: The vast majority of revenue sits in companies no one’s heard of.
insights.locator: Becoming a hostage to the logo

insights.claim: The worst lighthouse outcome is a prestigious customer who will not collaborate on repeatable software, will not pay recurring revenue, or will not pay a high enough ACV — turning the startup into a consulting shop that traded time for a vanity metric.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Check whether marquee-logo revenue is recurring and productized, or services revenue dressed as ARR.
insights.locator: Prestige without payback

insights.claim: Six-month POCs that never convert are a systematic trap because big logos love pilots; the fix is time-boxed pilots with clear milestones and auto-converting contracts.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Pilot-to-paid conversion terms are a concrete diligence item that separates real pipeline from pilot purgatory.
insights.quote: The fix is time-boxed pilots with clear milestones and auto-converting contracts.
insights.locator: Pilot purgatory

insights.claim: Landgrab companies die of indigestion without qualification discipline and a deal desk — waking up with 200 customers and 50 underwater — and scaling coverage before the product is ready creates detractors at scale.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: In volume AI motions, churn cohorts and underwater-account share matter more than logo count; reputation damage compounds nonlinearly.
insights.quote: 50 unhappy customers means churn. 500 is a reputation problem.
insights.locator: Grabbing land you can’t hold

insights.claim: Landgrab founders mistake the valley for the market: canvassing every bus stop in a major metro is not grabbing land, and the real opportunity is showing ROI to the 50,000 companies outside normal networks.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Distribution reach into non-coastal, non-networked buyers is the durable moat in landgrab AI — favors companies that build outbound machinery early.
insights.quote: The real opportunity is figuring out how to show your ROI to the 50,000 companies outside of normal networks.
insights.locator: Mistaking the valley for the market

insights.claim: The best companies sequence deliberately from lighthouse to landgrab — winning a bellwether in one vertical, dominating it, then moving to structurally similar adjacent verticals — as Affirm did by winning Casper, then every mattress company, then exercise equipment, then categories that only resembled it in being big-ticket installment purchases.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: Vertical adjacency should be defined by purchase-behavior similarity, not industry classification — a repeatable expansion template to test in portfolio companies.
insights.quote: Mattresses and Pelotons have nothing in common except that they’re big-ticket items people want to pay for over time, and Affirm saw that before the market did.
insights.locator: Sequencing: Lighthouse to Landgrab

insights.claim: The observable signal that a company has earned the transition to landgrab is buyers approaching it with allocated budgets and asking for a demo rather than asking who went first; going wide before the category is established burns cash and credibility.
insights.speaker: Joe Schmidt, Julian Marx
insights.so_what: A clean trigger for when to underwrite a sales-headcount step-up in an AI company — inbound with budget, not inbound curiosity.
insights.quote: The signal that you’ve earned it is buyers approaching you with allocated budgets and asking for a demo rather than asking who went first.
insights.locator: Eventually, new categories turn into recognized ones
